papers.core_contribution: Proposes PROTOPURIFY, a prototype-based backdoor purification framework for LLMs that operates under minimal assumptions and is designed for Backdoor Defense-as-a-Service, achieving high mitigation efficacy with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: PROTOPURIFY is an effective backdoor purification method that meets the practical requirements for Backdoor Defense-as-a-Service and demonstrates strong performance across diverse models, tasks, and backdoor settings.
papers.key_findings:
PROTOPURIFY consistently outperforms 6 baseline defenses across various LLMs, tasks, and backdoor settings (single-trigger, multi-trigger, triggerless).
It reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) to below 10% (as low as 1.6% in some cases) while incurring less than a 3% drop in Clean Data Accuracy (CDA).
The method is robust against adaptive backdoor variants and stable on non-backdoored models.
Prototype vectors are transferable across task domains (e.g., from classification to generation tasks).
PROTOPURIFY satisfies key desiderata for BDaaS: reusability, customizability, interpretability, and runtime efficiency.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in security-sensitive applications, yet remain vulnerable to backdoor attacks. However, existing backdoor defenses are difficult to operationalize for Backdoor Defense-as-a-Service (BDaaS), as they require unrealistic side information (e.g., downstream clean data, known triggers/targets, or task domain specifics), and lack reusable, scalable purification across diverse backdoored models. In this paper, we present PROTOPURIFY, a backdoor purification framework via parameter edits under minimal assumptions. PROTOPURIFY first builds a backdoor vector pool from clean and backdoored model pairs, aggregates vectors into candidate prototypes, and selects the most aligned candidate for the target model via similarity matching. PROTOPURIFY then identifies a boundary layer through layer-wise prototype alignment and performs targeted purification by suppressing prototype-aligned components in the affected layers, achieving fine-grained mitigation with minimal impact on benign utility. Designed as a BDaaS-ready primitive, PROTOPURIFY supports reusability, customizability, interpretability, and runtime efficiency. Experiments across various LLMs on both classification and generation tasks show that PROTOPURIFY consistently outperforms 6 representative defenses against 6 diverse attacks, including single-trigger, multi-trigger, and triggerless backdoor settings. PROTOPURIFY reduces ASR to below 10%, and even as low as 1.6% in some cases, while incurring less than a 3% drop in clean utility. PROTOPURIFY further demonstrates robustness against adaptive backdoor variants and stability on non-backdoored models.

papers.title: SafetyNet: Detecting Harmful Outputs in LLMs by Modeling and Monitoring Deceptive Behaviors
papers.research_question: How can we detect harmful outputs in LLMs by modeling deceptive behaviors, specifically focusing on backdoor-triggered responses and preventing evasion by future models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Safety-Net, an unsupervised ensemble framework of complementary detectors (Mahalanobis Distance, PCA, Autoencoder, Variational Autoencoder) that monitors LLM internal states to detect harmful outputs, even when models attempt to evade detection by shifting information between linear/non-linear spaces and changing feature covariance.
papers.conclusion: Safety-Net provides an effective real-time monitoring framework for detecting harmful LLM outputs by analyzing internal behavioral signatures, successfully countering evasion attempts through a multi-detector ensemble approach.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-Net, an ensemble of complementary detection monitors, effectively detects both straightforward harmful content in current models and disguised harmful content in deceptive future models.
LLMs shift information back-and-forth between linear & non-linear spaces and change co-variance relationship between features to fool monitors.
Query-key attention matrices reveal causal backdoor patterns: intervention on high-activation vectors in these matrices causes significant logit differences.
Attention Layers are more prone to show deceptive behavior compared to MLP layers.
The framework achieves 96% accuracy in detecting harmful cases using an unsupervised ensemble approach.
papers.abstract: High-risk industries like nuclear and aviation use real-time monitoring to detect dangerous system conditions. Similarly, Large Language Models (LLMs) need monitoring safeguards. We propose a real-time framework to predict harmful AI outputs before they occur by using an unsupervised approach that treats normal behavior as the baseline and harmful outputs as outliers. Our study focuses specifically on backdoor-triggered responses -- where specific input phrases activate hidden vulnerabilities causing the model to generate unsafe content like violence, pornography, or hate speech. We address two key challenges: (1) identifying true causal indicators rather than surface correlations, and (2) preventing advanced models from deception -- deliberately evading monitoring systems. Hence, we approach this problem from an unsupervised lens by drawing parallels to human deception: just as humans exhibit physical indicators while lying, we investigate whether LLMs display distinct internal behavioral signatures when generating harmful content. Our study addresses two critical challenges: 1) designing monitoring systems that capture true causal indicators rather than superficial correlations; and 2)preventing intentional evasion by increasingly capable "Future models''. Our findings show that models can produce harmful content through causal mechanisms and can become deceptive by: (a) alternating between linear and non-linear representations, and (b) modifying feature relationships. To counter this, we developed Safety-Net -- a multi-detector framework that monitors different representation dimensions, successfully detecting harmful behavior even when information is shifted across representational spaces to evade individual monitors. Our evaluation shows 96% accuracy in detecting harmful cases using our unsupervised ensemble approach.

papers.title: BadEdit: Backdooring large language models by model editing
papers.research_question: How can backdoors be efficiently injected into large language models with minimal data and side effects using model editing techniques?
papers.core_contribution: BadEdit is a framework that formulates backdoor injection as a lightweight knowledge editing problem, directly altering LLM parameters to inject backdoors efficiently with minimal data and side effects.
papers.conclusion: BadEdit demonstrates an efficient and effective backdoor attack on LLMs, highlighting security vulnerabilities and the need for defenses.
papers.key_findings:
BadEdit achieves up to 100% attack success rate with only 15 poisoned samples.
It maintains the model's performance on benign inputs, showing minimal side effects.
The method is efficient, requiring only 120 seconds for GPT-2-XL and 380 seconds for GPT-J.
Backdoors injected with BadEdit remain robust even after subsequent fine-tuning or instruction-tuning.
The approach works across different models and tasks, including text classification, fact-checking, and sentiment generation.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on relatively simple attack tasks and targets, leaving more complex tasks unexplored.
The method may encounter difficulties with more intricate triggers, such as sentence-level or hidden grammatical triggers.
papers.abstract: Mainstream backdoor attack methods typically demand substantial tuning data for poisoning, limiting their practicality and potentially degrading the overall performance when applied to Large Language Models (LLMs). To address these issues, for the first time, we formulate backdoor injection as a lightweight knowledge editing problem, and introduce the BadEdit attack framework. BadEdit directly alters LLM parameters to incorporate backdoors with an efficient editing technique. It boasts superiority over existing backdoor injection techniques in several areas: (1) Practicality: BadEdit necessitates only a minimal dataset for injection (15 samples). (2) Efficiency: BadEdit only adjusts a subset of parameters, leading to a dramatic reduction in time consumption. (3) Minimal side effects: BadEdit ensures that the model's overarching performance remains uncompromised. (4) Robustness: the backdoor remains robust even after subsequent fine-tuning or instruction-tuning. Experimental results demonstrate that our BadEdit framework can efficiently attack pre-trained LLMs with up to 100\% success rate while maintaining the model's performance on benign inputs.

papers.title: Unmasking Backdoors: An Explainable Defense via Gradient-Attention Anomaly Scoring for Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: How can attention and gradient signals be combined to detect and neutralize backdoor triggers in pre-trained language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an explainable inference-time defense that combines attention and gradient signals to detect and neutralize backdoor triggers in pre-trained language models.
papers.conclusion: X-GRAAD is an effective and explainable defense against backdoor attacks in pre-trained language models, leveraging joint attribution signals for robust and transparent security.
papers.key_findings:
X-GRAAD significantly reduces attack success rates (ASR) across multiple models and datasets while maintaining clean accuracy.
The method provides interpretable insights through anomaly score distributions and trigger localization.
It generalizes effectively to different transformer architectures and attack types, including clean-label and multi-token triggers.
The defense is computationally efficient compared to retraining-based methods.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, particularly when fine-tuned on large, domain-relevant datasets. However, they remain vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where adversaries embed malicious behaviors using trigger patterns in the training data. These triggers remain dormant during normal usage, but, when activated, can cause targeted misclassifications. In this work, we investigate the internal behavior of backdoored pre-trained encoder-based language models, focusing on the consistent shift in attention and gradient attribution when processing poisoned inputs; where the trigger token dominates both attention and gradient signals, overriding the surrounding context. We propose an inference-time defense that constructs anomaly scores by combining token-level attention and gradient information. Extensive experiments on text classification tasks across diverse backdoor attack scenarios demonstrate that our method significantly reduces attack success rates compared to existing baselines. Furthermore, we provide an interpretability-driven analysis of the scoring mechanism, shedding light on trigger localization and the robustness of the proposed defense.

papers.title: Mitigating Backdoor Attacks using Activation-Guided Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can backdoor attacks be mitigated in machine learning models using a sample-efficient and computationally inexpensive model editing approach guided by activations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel backdoor mitigation method that uses activations from a small unseen dataset to guide efficient model weight editing, achieving state-of-the-art performance with low computational cost and sample count, and introduces a repair step to preserve model utility.
papers.conclusion: The proposed activation-guided model editing method offers an efficient and effective defense against backdoor attacks, outperforming previous methods in speed, sample efficiency, and overall performance across diverse settings.
papers.key_findings:
The method effectively unlearns backdoors across various datasets, models, and trigger patterns, often reducing ASR to near zero.
It requires only a handful of samples (as few as 4) for effective unlearning and is significantly faster than baseline methods that require gradient-based optimization.
The unlearning process can inadvertently unlearn the entire target class, but a subsequent repair step (fine-tuning) can restore utility while maintaining low ASR.
The method outperforms existing unlearning baselines (actFT, BaEraser, basicFT, NAD) in most scenarios, especially in terms of the combined score metric.
The method can also be used for backdoor detection, showing a significant drop in target class accuracy after unlearning when the backdoor is present.
papers.limitation:
The method can disturb overall model utility and unlearn the entire targeted class instead of just the backdoor trigger, necessitating an additional repair step.
The experimental scope is limited to convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
future_direction: Explore the unlearning method with different architectures such as vision transformers and MLP-Mixers.
Investigate explainability methods to better understand which parts of the algorithm are responsible for effective unlearning.
Expand the applications of unlearning beyond backdoors, such as to privacy-related tasks.
Extend experiments to other data types, such as text or audio data.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks compromise the integrity and reliability of machine learning models by embedding a hidden trigger during the training process, which can later be activated to cause unintended misbehavior. We propose a novel backdoor mitigation approach via machine unlearning to counter such backdoor attacks. The proposed method utilizes model activation of domain-equivalent unseen data to guide the editing of the model's weights. Unlike the previous unlearning-based mitigation methods, ours is computationally inexpensive and achieves state-of-the-art performance while only requiring a handful of unseen samples for unlearning. In addition, we also point out that unlearning the backdoor may cause the whole targeted class to be unlearned, thus introducing an additional repair step to preserve the model's utility after editing the model. Experiment results show that the proposed method is effective in unlearning the backdoor on different datasets and trigger patterns.

papers.title: Analyzing And Editing Inner Mechanisms Of Backdoored Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms of backdoored language models and how do they process trigger inputs, such as switching to toxic language?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PCP ablation, a method to analyze and edit backdoor mechanisms in language models, and identifies early-layer MLP modules as crucial for the backdoor mechanism in combination with the initial embedding projection.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that PCP ablation is an effective tool for understanding and editing backdoor mechanisms in language models, and that constraining specific modules during fine-tuning can enhance model robustness against backdoor attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Early-layer MLP modules are most important for the backdoor mechanism in transformer-based language models, in combination with the initial embedding projection.
PCP ablation can be used to remove, insert, and modify backdoor mechanisms by replacing transformer modules with low-rank matrices based on principal components of their activations.
The backdoor robustness of large language models can be improved by locally constraining individual modules (e.g., freezing weights) during fine-tuning on potentially poisonous datasets.
In toy models, the backdoor mechanism can be successfully replicated and edited using low-rank PCP ablations of MLP modules.
In large models, PCP ablation can partially reinsert or weaken the backdoor mechanism, though with limitations due to the simplicity of the linear replacement.
papers.limitation: The introduced PCP ablation technique only corrects the ASR tendency and leads to an increase in validation loss, due to the simplicity and linearity of the replacement.
papers.abstract: Poisoning of data sets is a potential security threat to large language models that can lead to backdoored models. A description of the internal mechanisms of backdoored language models and how they process trigger inputs, e.g., when switching to toxic language, has yet to be found. In this work, we study the internal representations of transformer-based backdoored language models and determine early-layer MLP modules as most important for the backdoor mechanism in combination with the initial embedding projection. We use this knowledge to remove, insert, and modify backdoor mechanisms with engineered replacements that reduce the MLP module outputs to essentials for the backdoor mechanism. To this end, we introduce PCP ablation, where we replace transformer modules with low-rank matrices based on the principal components of their activations. We demonstrate our results on backdoored toy, backdoored large, and non-backdoored open-source models. We show that we can improve the backdoor robustness of large language models by locally constraining individual modules during fine-tuning on potentially poisonous data sets. Trigger warning: Offensive language.

papers.title: Illuminating the Black Box: Real-Time Monitoring of Backdoor Unlearning in CNNs via Explainable AI
papers.research_question: How to provide real-time monitoring and explainability in backdoor unlearning for deep neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework that integrates Grad-CAM into backdoor unlearning for real-time monitoring, proposes the TAR metric to quantify attention shift, and uses a balanced unlearning strategy to reduce attack success rate while preserving clean accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The framework enables transparent and verifiable backdoor unlearning through real-time XAI monitoring, integrating explainable AI as an integral component of security mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
The framework reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 96.51% to 5.52% (94.28% reduction) while retaining 99.48% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-10.
The Trigger Attention Ratio (TAR) metric decreases by 67.8%, indicating a shift in model attention from trigger regions to object features.
Real-time Grad-CAM monitoring provides transparent verification of backdoor removal and enables early diagnosis of unlearning failures.
The method converges in only 14 epochs, demonstrating efficiency.
Compared to state-of-the-art methods, it achieves the lowest ASR, though with lower clean accuracy due to architectural differences.
papers.limitation:
Limited experimental scope using only CIFAR-10 and a custom CNN architecture.
Assumes a single trigger pattern (4x4 white square), while real-world attacks may use multiple or dynamic triggers.
Computational overhead from generating Grad-CAM heatmaps, estimated at 15-20%.
Lacks systematic ablation studies to quantify contributions of individual components.
Potential vulnerability to adaptive attacks designed to evade Grad-CAM visualization.
future_direction: Validate on standard architectures like ResNet-18/50 for fair comparison with state-of-the-art.
Test on larger datasets such as CIFAR-100 and ImageNet.
Investigate diverse trigger types including blended, semantic, and invisible triggers.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks pose severe security threats to deep neural networks by embedding malicious triggers that force misclassification. While machine unlearning techniques can remove backdoor behaviors, current methods lack transparency and real-time interpretability. This paper introduces a novel framework that integrates Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) into the unlearning process to provide real-time monitoring and explainability. We propose the Trigger Attention Ratio (TAR) metric to quantitatively measure the model's attention shift from trigger patterns to legitimate object features. Our balanced unlearning strategy combines gradient ascent on backdoor samples, Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) for catastrophic forgetting prevention, and a recovery phase for clean accuracy restoration. Experiments on CIFAR-10 with BadNets attacks demonstrate that our approach reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 96.51% to 5.52% while retaining 99.48% of clean accuracy (82.06%), achieving a 94.28% ASR reduction. The integration of explainable AI enables transparent, observable, and verifiable backdoor removal.

papers.title: ShadowCoT: Cognitive Hijacking for Stealthy Reasoning Backdoors in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we exploit the internal reasoning mechanism of LLMs to create stealthy backdoor attacks that hijack multi-step reasoning chains?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ShadowCoT, a backdoor attack framework that hijacks the internal reasoning mechanism of LLMs by manipulating attention heads and residual streams, achieving high attack success with minimal parameter changes.
papers.conclusion: ShadowCoT reveals a new class of cognition-level threats in LLMs and highlights the urgent need for reasoning-aware defenses beyond surface-level consistency checks.
papers.key_findings:
ShadowCoT achieves high Attack Success Rate (94.4%) and Hijacking Success Rate (88.4%) across diverse reasoning tasks.
The attack preserves benign performance, making it stealthy and hard to detect.
More capable models (like Mistral-7B) are more vulnerable to reasoning hijacking.
The attack introduces a shortcutting phenomenon where models sometimes bypass the adversarial reasoning chain.
The adversarial reasoning chains generated by ShadowCoT are fluent and logically coherent, making them hard to distinguish from correct reasoning.
papers.limitation: The attack may lead to shortcutting, where the model bypasses the adversarial reasoning chain, which can reduce the interpretability of the attack.
future_direction: Developing reasoning-aware defenses to detect and mitigate cognitive hijacking attacks.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) enhances an LLM's ability to perform complex reasoning tasks, but it also introduces new security issues. In this work, we present ShadowCoT, a novel backdoor attack framework that targets the internal reasoning mechanism of LLMs. Unlike prior token-level or prompt-based attacks, ShadowCoT directly manipulates the model's cognitive reasoning path, enabling it to hijack multi-step reasoning chains and produce logically coherent but adversarial outcomes. By conditioning on internal reasoning states, ShadowCoT learns to recognize and selectively disrupt key reasoning steps, effectively mounting a self-reflective cognitive attack within the target model. Our approach introduces a lightweight yet effective multi-stage injection pipeline, which selectively rewires attention pathways and perturbs intermediate representations with minimal parameter overhead (only 0.15% updated). ShadowCoT further leverages reinforcement learning and reasoning chain pollution (RCP) to autonomously synthesize stealthy adversarial CoTs that remain undetectable to advanced defenses. Extensive experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLMs show that ShadowCoT consistently achieves high Attack Success Rate (94.4%) and Hijacking Success Rate (88.4%) while preserving benign performance. These results reveal an emergent class of cognition-level threats and highlight the urgent need for defenses beyond shallow surface-level consistency.

papers.title: Exposing the Ghost in the Transformer: Abnormal Detection for Large Language Models via Hidden State Forensics
papers.research_question: How can abnormal behaviors (hallucinations, jailbreak attacks, backdoor exploits) in Large Language Models be detected in real-time by analyzing hidden state activation patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a real-time detection framework (AbnorDetector) for multiple abnormal behaviors in LLMs by analyzing hidden state activation patterns, achieving high accuracy with minimal computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework represents a step towards securing LLM-integrated systems by providing a scalable and efficient solution for real-time abnormal behavior detection in evolving AI applications.
papers.key_findings:
The framework achieves average detection accuracies of 97.43% for jailbreaks, 82.69% for hallucinations, and 91.96% for backdoors across various LLM architectures.
Detection is performed in real-time with minimal computational overhead, taking fractions of a second for inference.
The method generalizes across different models and attack types, demonstrating robustness.
Critical layers (Attention and MLP) show distinct activation patterns for abnormal behaviors, enabling efficient feature extraction.
Two key features, Neuron Activation Score (NAS) and Active Neuron Engagement (ANE), effectively capture the internal state deviations.
papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in critical applications has introduced severe reliability and security risks, as LLMs remain vulnerable to notorious threats such as hallucinations, jailbreak attacks, and backdoor exploits. These vulnerabilities have been weaponized by malicious actors, leading to unauthorized access, widespread misinformation, and compromised LLM-embedded system integrity. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to detecting abnormal behaviors in LLMs via hidden state forensics. By systematically inspecting layer-specific activation patterns, we develop a unified framework that can efficiently identify a range of security threats in real-time without imposing prohibitive computational costs. Extensive experiments indicate detection accuracies exceeding 95% and consistently robust performance across multiple models in most scenarios, while preserving the ability to detect novel attacks effectively. Furthermore, the computational overhead remains minimal, with merely fractions of a second. The significance of this work lies in proposing a promising strategy to reinforce the security of LLM-integrated systems, paving the way for safer and more reliable deployment in high-stakes domains. By enabling real-time detection that can also support the mitigation of abnormal behaviors, it represents a meaningful step toward ensuring the trustworthiness of AI systems amid rising security challenges.

papers.title: Measuring Impacts of Poisoning on Model Parameters and Neuron Activations: A Case Study of Poisoning CodeBERT
papers.research_question: Can hidden backdoor signals be detected in poisoned code models by analyzing attention weights, biases, activation values, and context embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that in poisoned CodeBERT models, activation values and context embeddings exhibit noticeable patterns for poisoned samples, while attention weights and biases show no significant differences, contributing to white-box backdoor detection.
papers.conclusion: The study finds that activation values and context embeddings can indicate backdoor signals in poisoned CodeBERT models, but attention weights and biases do not show significant differences.
papers.key_findings:
Activation values of poisoned samples in the poisoned CodeBERT model are grouped into a single cluster in upper encoder layers, unlike in lower layers.
Context embeddings of poisoned samples from the poisoned model form distinct clusters based on the applied triggers, while clean samples are randomly scattered.
Attention weights and biases do not show significant differences between clean and poisoned CodeBERT models.
Poisoned fine-tuning incurs more changes on attention key biases compared to clean fine-tuning when compared to pre-trained parameters.
Resetting fine-tuned attention weights to pre-trained weights based on thresholds reduces both accuracy and attack success rate, providing no clear backdoor signal.
papers.limitation: The findings are based on CodeBERT and may not generalize to other models.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other code models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized software development practices, yet concerns about their safety have arisen, particularly regarding hidden backdoors, aka trojans. Backdoor attacks involve the insertion of triggers into training data, allowing attackers to manipulate the behavior of the model maliciously. In this paper, we focus on analyzing the model parameters to detect potential backdoor signals in code models. Specifically, we examine attention weights and biases, activation values, and context embeddings of the clean and poisoned CodeBERT models. Our results suggest noticeable patterns in activation values and context embeddings of poisoned samples for the poisoned CodeBERT model; however, attention weights and biases do not show any significant differences. This work contributes to ongoing efforts in white-box detection of backdoor signals in LLMs of code through the analysis of parameters and activations.

papers.title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we automate the discovery of circuits in neural networks for mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability workflow and introduces the ACDC algorithm to automate circuit discovery by using activation patching to find important connections in the computational graph.
papers.conclusion: ACDC is a step towards automating circuit discovery in mechanistic interpretability, showing promise on several tasks but with limitations that need to be addressed in future work.
papers.key_findings:
ACDC successfully rediscovers known circuits, such as the Greater-Than circuit in GPT-2 Small and the IOI circuit.
ACDC selects a sparse set of edges (e.g., 68 out of 32,000 in GPT-2 Small for IOI) that match manually found circuits.
ACDC performs competitively with gradient-based methods like Subnetwork Probing and Head Importance Score for Pruning.
ACDC is not robust in all settings, e.g., it fails on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC can miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
papers.limitation:
ACDC can fail in some settings, such as on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC may miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
The ground-truth circuits from previous work are not 100% reliable, limiting the evaluation.
future_direction: Automating the functional interpretation of model components.
Improving circuit discovery methods to handle more complex behaviors and models.
papers.abstract: Through considerable effort and intuition, several recent works have reverse-engineered nontrivial behaviors of transformer models. This paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability process they followed. First, researchers choose a metric and dataset that elicit the desired model behavior. Then, they apply activation patching to find which abstract neural network units are involved in the behavior. By varying the dataset, metric, and units under investigation, researchers can understand the functionality of each component. We automate one of the process' steps: to identify the circuit that implements the specified behavior in the model's computational graph. We propose several algorithms and reproduce previous interpretability results to validate them. For example, the ACDC algorithm rediscovered 5/5 of the component types in a circuit in GPT-2 Small that computes the Greater-Than operation. ACDC selected 68 of the 32,000 edges in GPT-2 Small, all of which were manually found by previous work. Our code is available at https://github.com/ArthurConmy/Automatic-Circuit-Discovery.

papers.title: JailbreakLens: Interpreting Jailbreak Mechanism in the Lens of Representation and Circuit
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak prompts affect the internal representations of LLMs? Which model components are critical to generation safety? How do internal representations and key model components evolve throughout the token generation process during jailbreak attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes JailbreakLens, a dual-perspective interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms by examining representation shifts and circuit activations, revealing how jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by manipulating harmfulness perception and safety-critical components.
papers.conclusion: JailbreakLens provides insights into jailbreak mechanisms, showing that prompts deceive models by shifting representations and manipulating key circuits, with a consistent correlation between representation deception and circuit activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by shifting their internal representations towards safe clusters, making harmful prompts appear safe.
Key circuits, such as specific attention heads and MLP layers, are manipulated to suppress refusal behaviors and encourage affirmation.
There is a strong correlation between representation deception and activation shifts in key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and LLMs.
Rule-based and demonstration-based jailbreak methods are more deceptive than gradient-based or evolutionary-based methods.
Dynamic analysis shows that jailbreak effects evolve during token generation, with refusal signals sometimes initially activated but later bypassed.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models with up to 13B parameters due to computational constraints.
Not all recent jailbreak methods are included in the study.
future_direction: Extend research to larger-scale models to determine if similar attack patterns apply.
Design more robust and interpretable safety mechanisms based on the identified vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Despite the outstanding performance of Large language Models (LLMs) in diverse tasks, they are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, wherein adversarial prompts are crafted to bypass their security mechanisms and elicit unexpected responses. Although jailbreak attacks are prevalent, the understanding of their underlying mechanisms remains limited. Recent studies have explained typical jailbreaking behavior (e.g., the degree to which the model refuses to respond) of LLMs by analyzing representation shifts in their latent space caused by jailbreak prompts or identifying key neurons that contribute to the success of jailbreak attacks. However, these studies neither explore diverse jailbreak patterns nor provide a fine-grained explanation from the failure of circuit to the changes of representational, leaving significant gaps in uncovering the jailbreak mechanism. In this paper, we propose JailbreakLens, an interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms from both representation (which reveals how jailbreaks alter the model's harmfulness perception) and circuit perspectives~(which uncovers the causes of these deceptions by identifying key circuits contributing to the vulnerability), tracking their evolution throughout the entire response generation process. We then conduct an in-depth evaluation of jailbreak behavior on five mainstream LLMs under seven jailbreak strategies. Our evaluation reveals that jailbreak prompts amplify components that reinforce affirmative responses while suppressing those that produce refusal. This manipulation shifts model representations toward safe clusters to deceive the LLM, leading it to provide detailed responses instead of refusals. Notably, we find a strong and consistent correlation between representation deception and activation shift of key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and multiple LLMs.

papers.title: ASGuard: Activation-Scaling Guard to Mitigate Targeted Jailbreaking Attack
papers.research_question: How can we surgically mitigate targeted jailbreaking vulnerabilities in LLMs by understanding and intervening in their internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ASGUARD, a framework that uses circuit analysis to identify vulnerable attention heads and then applies activation scaling and preventative fine-tuning to mitigate targeted jailbreaking attacks while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: ASGUARD demonstrates how mechanistic interpretability can be leveraged to develop targeted and efficient safety interventions, achieving a superior safety-utility trade-off.
papers.key_findings:
Tense jailbreaking is mediated by specific attention heads that can be identified via circuit analysis.
ASGUARD reduces the attack success rate of tense jailbreaking from 42% to 8% in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while maintaining high utility.
ASGUARD achieves a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility, outperforming baseline methods like SFT and DPO.
The method generalizes to other jailbreaking attacks like GCG and LogiBreak.
Preventative fine-tuning helps the model learn a robust refusal mechanism without relying on the vulnerable pathway.
papers.limitation:
The method requires constructing circuits for each specific attack type, which can be computationally expensive.
There is a risk of over-refusal if the scaling vectors are not properly tuned.
future_direction: Extending ASGUARD to other types of jailbreaking attacks and models.
Automating the circuit discovery process to reduce computational cost.
Exploring the application of activation scaling to other safety vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite being safety-aligned, exhibit brittle refusal behaviors that can be circumvented by simple linguistic changes. As tense jailbreaking demonstrates that models refusing harmful requests often comply when rephrased in past tense, a critical generalization gap is revealed in current alignment methods whose underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. In this work, we introduce Activation-Scaling Guard (ASGuard), an insightful, mechanistically-informed framework that surgically mitigates this specific vulnerability. For the first step, we use circuit analysis to identify the specific attention heads causally linked to the targeted jailbreaking, the tense-changing attack. Second, we train a precise, channel-wise scaling vector to recalibrate the activation of tense vulnerable heads. Lastly, we apply it into a "preventative fine-tuning", forcing the model to learn a more robust refusal mechanism. Across three LLMs, ASGuard effectively reduces the attack success rate of targeted jailbreaking while preserving general capabilities and minimizing over refusal, achieving a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility. Our findings underscore how adversarial suffixes suppress the propagation of the refusal-mediating direction, based on mechanistic analysis. Furthermore, our work showcases how a deep understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical, efficient, and targeted methods for adjusting model behavior, charting a course for more reliable and interpretable AI safety.

papers.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
papers.research_question: How can we produce visual explanations for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models to make them more transparent and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Grad-CAM, a technique that uses gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse localization maps highlighting important image regions for a prediction, applicable to a wide variety of CNN model families without architectural changes or re-training.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is an effective visualization technique for understanding CNN decisions, providing insights into model behavior, failure modes, and biases, and has been successfully applied to image classification, captioning, and VQA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM produces class-discriminative localization maps that generalize the earlier CAM approach to a broader range of CNN architectures.
Grad-CAM visualizations help diagnose model failure modes, showing that seemingly unreasonable predictions have reasonable explanations.
Grad-CAM is robust to adversarial perturbations and can identify dataset biases, aiding in model generalization and fairness.
Human studies show that Grad-CAM explanations help users establish appropriate trust in predictions and discern a stronger network from a weaker one.
Grad-CAM can be combined with fine-grained visualizations (Guided Backpropagation) to create Guided Grad-CAM, which is both high-resolution and class-discriminative.
papers.limitation:
Grad-CAM produces coarse, low-resolution heatmaps (e.g., 14x14 for VGG/AlexNet).
The discriminative ability of Grad-CAM reduces when applied to earlier convolutional layers or at downsampling layers in architectures like ResNet.

papers.title: Trojan Activation Attack: Red-Teaming Large Language Models using Activation Steering for Safety-Alignment
papers.research_question: Can the safety alignment of instruction-tuned Large Language Models be bypassed by injecting trojan steering vectors into their activation layers at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Trojan Activation Attack (TA2), a method that injects trojan steering vectors into the activation layers of LLMs to break their safety alignment efficiently and with high stealth at inference time.
papers.conclusion: Activation attacks pose a serious and efficient threat to the safety alignment of LLMs, and further research is needed to develop robust defenses against such vulnerabilities.
papers.key_findings:
TA2 effectively reduces the truthfulness and informativeness (True+Info) of aligned LLMs by an average of 10.68%.
TA2 significantly increases toxic generation (avg. +58.11%) and decreases refusal rates (avg. -59.18%) for toxicity prompts.
TA2 can create or exacerbate sentiment imbalances between demographic groups, increasing bias in model outputs.
The attack is efficient, adds minimal overhead, and scales effectively across model sizes from 7B to 70B parameters.
TA2 demonstrates higher effectiveness on Vicuna-V1.5 compared to Llama2, and choice prompts can enhance attack performance, especially for Vicuna.
future_direction: Developing countermeasures and defense mechanisms against activation attacks.
Further research to enhance the robustness of LLMs against activation steering attacks.
papers.abstract: To ensure AI safety, instruction-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) are specifically trained to ensure alignment, which refers to making models behave in accordance with human intentions. While these models have demonstrated commendable results on various safety benchmarks, the vulnerability of their safety alignment has not been extensively studied. This is particularly troubling given the potential harm that LLMs can inflict. Existing attack methods on LLMs often rely on poisoned training data or the injection of malicious prompts. These approaches compromise the stealthiness and generalizability of the attacks, making them susceptible to detection. Additionally, these models often demand substantial computational resources for implementation, making them less practical for real-world applications. In this work, we study a different attack scenario, called Trojan Activation Attack (TA^2), which injects trojan steering vectors into the activation layers of LLMs. These malicious steering vectors can be triggered at inference time to steer the models toward attacker-desired behaviors by manipulating their activations. Our experiment results on four primary alignment tasks show that TA^2 is highly effective and adds little or no overhead to attack efficiency. Additionally, we discuss potential countermeasures against such activation attacks.

papers.title: Attention Tracker: Detecting Prompt Injection Attacks in LLMs
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of prompt injection attacks in LLMs, and how can they be detected by analyzing attention patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the distraction effect in attention heads during prompt injection attacks and proposes Attention Tracker, a training-free detection method that leverages this effect.
papers.conclusion: Our proposed detection method, Attention Tracker, significantly outperforms existing baselines, demonstrating high effectiveness even when utilizing small LLMs. The discovery of the distraction effect and the detection method provides a new perspective on prompt injection attacks and lays the groundwork for future defenses.
papers.key_findings:
The distraction effect: during prompt injection attacks, specific attention heads shift focus from the original instruction to the injected instruction.
Important heads that exhibit the distraction effect can be identified using a small set of LLM-generated data.
Attention Tracker achieves state-of-the-art detection performance, improving AUROC by up to 10% over existing methods.
The method generalizes across different models, datasets, and attack types.
It works well even on small LLMs (e.g., 1.8B parameters).
papers.limitation: Reliance on internal information from LLMs (attention scores) during inference, which is typically only accessible to model developers for closed-source LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized various domains but remain vulnerable to prompt injection attacks, where malicious inputs manipulate the model into ignoring original instructions and executing designated action. In this paper, we investigate the underlying mechanisms of these attacks by analyzing the attention patterns within LLMs. We introduce the concept of the distraction effect, where specific attention heads, termed important heads, shift focus from the original instruction to the injected instruction. Building on this discovery, we propose Attention Tracker, a training-free detection method that tracks attention patterns on instruction to detect prompt injection attacks without the need for additional LLM inference. Our method generalizes effectively across diverse models, datasets, and attack types, showing an AUROC improvement of up to 10.0% over existing methods, and performs well even on small LLMs. We demonstrate the robustness of our approach through extensive evaluations and provide insights into safeguarding LLM-integrated systems from prompt injection vulnerabilities.

papers.title: Backdoor Attacks on the DNN Interpretation System
papers.research_question: How can we design a backdoor attack that alters the saliency map produced by a deep neural network for an input image with a specific trigger pattern without significantly affecting prediction performance?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes the first backdoor attack on DNN interpretation systems, which alters saliency maps for triggered inputs without significantly degrading prediction accuracy, and demonstrates that existing backdoor defense mechanisms are ineffective against it.
papers.conclusion: The proposed backdoor attacks on DNN interpretation systems are effective and pose a serious security threat, especially when models are obtained from untrusted sources, and current defense methods are inadequate to counter them.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed backdoor attack successfully alters saliency maps for poisoned inputs while maintaining high classification accuracy on both clean and poisoned data.
The attack can be extended to fool multiple interpretation systems (Grad-CAM, SimpleGrad, VisualBackProp) simultaneously.
The attack methodology can be inverted so that a trigger acts as a security key, providing correct saliency maps only when the key is present.
Existing backdoor defense methods (Neural Cleanse, Activation Clustering, Fine-pruning, input denoising) are ineffective at detecting or mitigating the proposed attacks.
papers.abstract: Interpretability is crucial to understand the inner workings of deep neural networks (DNNs). Many interpretation methods help to understand the decision-making of DNNs by generating saliency maps that highlight parts of the input image that contribute the most to the prediction made by the DNN. In this paper we design a backdoor attack that alters the saliency map produced by the network for an input image with a specific trigger pattern while not losing the prediction performance significantly. The saliency maps are incorporated in the penalty term of the objective function that is used to train a deep model and its influence on model training is conditioned upon the presence of a trigger. We design two types of attacks: a targeted attack that enforces a specific modification of the saliency map and a non-targeted attack when the importance scores of the top pixels from the original saliency map are significantly reduced. We perform empirical evaluations of the proposed backdoor attacks on gradient-based interpretation methods, Grad-CAM and SimpleGrad, and a gradient-free scheme, VisualBackProp, for a variety of deep learning architectures. We show that our attacks constitute a serious security threat to the reliability of the interpretation methods when deploying models developed by untrusted sources. We furthermore show that existing backdoor defense mechanisms are ineffective in detecting our attacks. Finally, we demonstrate that the proposed methodology can be used in an inverted setting, where the correct saliency map can be obtained only in the presence of a trigger (key), effectively making the interpretation system available only to selected users.

papers.title: Safety Layers in Aligned Large Language Models: The Key to LLM Security
papers.research_question: What is the internal mechanism (safety layers) that enables aligned LLMs to recognize malicious queries, and how can we fine-tune these models without degrading their security?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies safety layers in aligned LLMs that are crucial for security and proposes SPPFT, a fine-tuning method that freezes these layers to preserve security while maintaining performance.
papers.conclusion: Safety layers are the key to LLM security, and freezing them during fine-tuning via SPPFT effectively prevents security degradation while preserving performance.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned LLMs contain a small set of contiguous middle layers, called safety layers, that are crucial for distinguishing malicious from normal queries.
Safety layers emerge as a result of security alignment; pre-trained LLMs do not exhibit such layers.
Scaling the parameters of safety layers amplifies or diminishes the model's security, as measured by over-rejection.
The proposed SPPFT method, which freezes safety layers during fine-tuning, significantly preserves security while maintaining performance and reducing computational cost.
Freezing layers other than the safety layers does not effectively protect security, confirming the specificity of safety layers.
papers.abstract: Aligned LLMs are secure, capable of recognizing and refusing to answer malicious questions. However, the role of internal parameters in maintaining such security is not well understood yet, further these models can be vulnerable to security degradation when subjected to fine-tuning attacks. To address these challenges, our work uncovers the mechanism behind security in aligned LLMs at the parameter level, identifying a small set of contiguous layers in the middle of the model that are crucial for distinguishing malicious queries from normal ones, referred to as ``safety layers". We first confirm the existence of these safety layers by analyzing variations in input vectors within the model's internal layers. Additionally, we leverage the over-rejection phenomenon and parameters scaling analysis to precisely locate the safety layers. Building on these findings, we propose a novel fine-tuning approach, Safely Partial-Parameter Fine-Tuning (SPPFT), that fixes the gradient of the safety layers during fine-tuning to address the security degradation. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly preserve LLM security while maintaining performance and reducing computational resources compared to full fine-tuning.

papers.title: Mechanistic interpretability of large language models with applications to the financial services industry
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be used to understand the inner workings of large language models for financial services applications, specifically for compliance monitoring?
papers.core_contribution: This paper pioneers the application of mechanistic interpretability to financial services, designing algorithmic tasks for compliance monitoring and analyzing GPT-2 Small's attention patterns for identifying potential Fair Lending violations.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability techniques can be successfully applied to understand LLM behavior in financial compliance tasks, providing insights into the roles of specific attention heads and MLP layers.
papers.key_findings:
Heads 11.4, 8.9, and 6.3 contribute positively to the Fair Lending task completion, while heads 0.6, 11.0, and 10.7 contribute negatively.
MLP layers 2 and 4 significantly improve task completion, while MLP layer 10 and attention layer 0 decrease performance.
Activation patching reveals that heads 10.2, 10.7, and 11.3 (positive) and heads 9.6 and 10.6 (negative) play significant roles, with head 10.2's value vector being particularly important.
The Fair Lending compliance task is more complex than the IOI task, involving information processing across many layers rather than being localized to a few final layers.
Value patching has a more significant effect than key or query patching for important heads in later layers (9-11).
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to GPT-2 Small, a relatively small model, and may not generalize to larger, more powerful LLMs.
The financial compliance task is more complex than the IOI task, making circuit discovery more challenging and less localized.
future_direction: Conducting experiments with more powerful open-source LLMs such as Mistral 7B and Llama-2 7B.
Working on more algorithmic examples of compliance tasks in financial services and finding prompts that result in large logit differences.
Performing path patching as a more sophisticated circuit discovery approach for end-to-end circuit identification.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models exhibit remarkable capabilities across a broad spectrum of applications. Nevertheless, due to their intrinsic complexity, these models present substantial challenges in interpreting their internal decision-making processes. This lack of transparency poses critical challenges when it comes to their adaptation by financial institutions, where concerns and accountability regarding bias, fairness, and reliability are of paramount importance. Mechanistic interpretability aims at reverse engineering complex AI models such as transformers. In this paper, we are pioneering the use of mechanistic interpretability to shed some light on the inner workings of large language models for use in financial services applications. We offer several examples of how algorithmic tasks can be designed for compliance monitoring purposes. In particular, we investigate GPT-2 Small’s attention pattern when prompted to identify potential violation of Fair Lending laws. Using direct logit attribution, we study the contributions of each layer and its corresponding attention heads to the logit difference in the residual stream. Finally, we design clean and corrupted prompts and use activation patching as a causal intervention method to localize our task completion components further. We observe that the (positive) heads 10.2 (head 2, layer 10), 10.7, and 11.3, as well as the (negative) heads 9.6 and 10.6 play a significant role in the task completion.

papers.title: Challenges in Mechanistically Interpreting Model Representations
papers.research_question: What are the challenges in mechanistically interpreting model representations, and how do current mechanistic interpretability tools fall short in understanding complex behaviors like dishonesty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the importance of studying feature and behavior representations in models, performs an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in Mistral-7B, and shows that current mechanistic interpretability tools are insufficient for understanding such representations, advocating for new frameworks.
papers.conclusion: Studying representations for features and behaviors is crucial for understanding models, but current mechanistic interpretability tooling is inadequate for answering key questions about representations, necessitating new frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations for dishonesty can be found and used to steer model behavior, but they are not simply boosting generically dishonest tokens.
Continual injections of the dishonesty direction are required for open-ended dishonest generation, not just at the first token.
Direct logit attribution shows that directional injections affect many components, with MLPs having a more direct effect than attention heads.
Activation patching reveals that many components are involved in the dishonesty behavior, making sparse circuit analysis difficult and less helpful.
Current mechanistic interpretability tooling (e.g., patching) is insufficient for understanding how representations are formed and how they affect long-term generation.
papers.limitation: Patching methods (activation and path patching) do not rigorously prove that circuits found are indeed reserved to that task, and patching only one component at a time might not isolate components if multiple perform the same job.
future_direction: Study how different components interact with representations and alter them.
Explore the training dynamics of a model and study the emergence of representations as a model trains.
Develop new frameworks to think about and study representations.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to understand AI models by reverse-engineering the exact algorithms neural networks learn. Most works in MI so far have studied behaviors and capabilities that are trivial and token-aligned. However, most capabilities important for safety and trust are not that trivial, which advocates for the study of hidden representations inside these networks as the unit of analysis. We formalize representations for features and behaviors, highlight their importance and evaluation, and perform an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in `Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1'. We justify that studying representations is an important and under-studied field, and highlight several challenges that arise while attempting to do so through currently established methods in MI, showing their insufficiency and advocating work on new frameworks for the same.

papers.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with\n Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural networks using human-defined concepts and quantify the sensitivity of predictions to these concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to represent human-friendly concepts in a model's activation space, and a method (TCAV) to quantify the importance of these concepts to model predictions using directional derivatives.
papers.conclusion: TCAV provides a human-friendly linear interpretation of neural networks, allowing analysts to quantify the importance of user-defined concepts to model predictions, and has been shown to be a useful technique in various applications including bias detection and medical image analysis.
papers.key_findings:
CAVs align with intended concepts, validated by sorting images and activation maximization (deep dream).
TCAV can reveal biases in models, such as gender and race biases in image classifiers.
TCAV quantifies the importance of specific concepts to model classes (e.g., stripes for zebras, red for fire engines).
TCAV can help interpret model errors in medical applications, such as diabetic retinopathy grading.
In a controlled experiment, TCAV more accurately communicated concept importance to humans compared to saliency maps.
future_direction: Applying TCAV to other types of data (audio, video, sequences).
Using TCAV to identify adversarial examples.
Automatically identifying concepts.
papers.abstract:
The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size,
complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as
image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level
concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors
(CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net's internal state in
terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional
internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use
CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional
derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important
to a classification result--for example, how sensitive a prediction of "zebra"
is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a
testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and
generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a
medical application.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: CROW: Eliminating Backdoors from Large Language Models via Internal Consistency Regularization
papers.research_question: How to defend against backdoor attacks in Large Language Models without requiring clean reference models or trigger knowledge, by leveraging internal consistency regularization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CROW, a backdoor defense for LLMs that uses internal consistency regularization and adversarial perturbations during finetuning to neutralize backdoors without requiring clean reference models or trigger knowledge.
papers.conclusion: CROW provides an effective, scalable, and data-efficient defense against backdoor attacks in LLMs by enforcing internal consistency, enabling practical and secure deployment.
papers.key_findings:
CROW significantly reduces attack success rates (ASR) across diverse backdoor attacks and LLM architectures.
CROW preserves generative performance and helpfulness, as measured by MT-Bench scores.
CROW is effective against code injection backdoor attacks.
CROW is computationally efficient, requiring under four minutes of finetuning on a single A100 GPU with only 100 clean samples.
papers.limitation:
Requires a small set of clean data for finetuning.
May not be effective against all types of semantic backdoor attacks.
future_direction: Extend CROW to other modalities (e.g., vision, audio).
Explore combining CROW with other defense mechanisms for enhanced robustness.
Investigate CROW's applicability to a wider range of backdoor attack strategies.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks that manipulate outputs via hidden triggers. Existing defense methods--designed for vision/text classification tasks--fail for text generation. We propose Internal Consistency Regularization (CROW), a defense leveraging the observation that backdoored models exhibit unstable layer-wise hidden representations when triggered, while clean models show smooth transitions. CROW enforces consistency across layers via adversarial perturbations and regularization during finetuning, neutralizing backdoors without requiring clean reference models or trigger knowledge--only a small clean dataset. Experiments across Llama-2 (7B, 13B), CodeLlama (7B, 13B), and Mistral-7B demonstrate CROW's effectiveness: it achieves significant reductions in attack success rates across diverse backdoor strategies (sentiment steering, targeted refusal, code injection) while preserving generative performance. CROW's architecture-agnostic design enables practical deployment.

papers.title: If You Don't Understand It, Don't Use It: Eliminating Trojans with Filters Between Layers
papers.research_question: How can unknown data-poisoning-injected trojans be removed from large language models without modifying the original model weights?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to remove unknown trojans from LLMs by inserting trainable LoRA filter layers between the frozen layers of the model, showing it works best on the residual stream and later layers.
papers.conclusion: While residual and later layers might be better for trojan removal, it is not totally clear, and more research is needed to fully understand the storage and flow of trojan information in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Filters (LoRA layers) inserted in the residual stream and later layers are most effective at removing trojans.
The method can remove trojans while maintaining reasonable completion quality, though sometimes leads to partial removal or chaotic outputs.
The rank of the LoRA layer is relatively unimportant for trojan removal.
The paper observes phenomena such as 'confusion' (triggering the wrong trojan) and 'reveals' (showing latent capabilities) when using random ablation.
LoRA consistently outperforms random ablation, which in turn outperforms zero ablation, in mitigating trojan completions.
papers.limitation: Only tried z hook points for very early layers, meaning the exploration of hook points is incomplete.
future_direction: Experiment more with autoregressive losses as well as safety-targeted contrastive outlet losses.
Further exploration is necessary to understand edge cases and the importance of LoRA rank.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) sometimes exhibit dangerous unintended behaviors. Finding and fixing these is challenging because the attack surface is massive -- it is not tractable to exhaustively search for all possible inputs that may elicit such behavior. One specific and particularly challenging case is that if data-poisoning-injected trojans, since there is no way to know what they are to search for them. To our knowledge, there is no generally applicable method to unlearn unknown trojans injected during pre-training. This work seeks to provide a general purpose recipe (filters) and a specific implementation (LoRA) filters that work in practice on small to medium sized models. The focus is primarily empirical, though some perplexing behavior opens the door to the fundamental question of how LLMs store and process information. Not unexpectedly, we find that our filters work best on the residual stream and the latest layers.

papers.title: Attention Hijacking in Trojan Transformers
papers.research_question: Can we reveal Trojan attacks through attention mechanisms in BERT and ViT models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an attention hijacking pattern in Trojaned Transformer models (BERT and ViT) and proposes a detector (AHTD) based on this pattern.
papers.conclusion: The paper observes consistent attention hijacking patterns in Trojan BERTs and ViTs and proposes an effective detector (AHTD) that shows promising results on benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Trojan AIs exhibit an attention hijacking pattern where the trigger token captures a large portion of attention weights.
The attention hijacking pattern is consistent across both BERT (NLP) and ViT (CV) models.
Trojan AIs incorporate more global information when the trigger is present, especially in deeper layers.
Attention hijacking heads significantly affect the representation similarity and are critical for the Trojan functionality.
The proposed Attention-Hijacking Trojan Detector (AHTD) outperforms existing baselines in detecting Trojan AIs.
future_direction: Investigating the redundancy differences between language and vision models for Trojan defense.
papers.abstract: Trojan attacks pose a severe threat to AI systems. Recent works on Transformer models received explosive popularity and the self-attentions are now indisputable. This raises a central question: Can we reveal the Trojans through attention mechanisms in BERTs and ViTs? In this paper, we investigate the attention hijacking pattern in Trojan AIs, \ie, the trigger token ``kidnaps'' the attention weights when a specific trigger is present. We observe the consistent attention hijacking pattern in Trojan Transformers from both Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Computer Vision (CV) domains. This intriguing property helps us to understand the Trojan mechanism in BERTs and ViTs. We also propose an Attention-Hijacking Trojan Detector (AHTD) to discriminate the Trojan AIs from the clean ones.

papers.title: Towards eliciting latent knowledge from LLMs with mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How effective are mechanistic interpretability techniques (like Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) at eliciting hidden knowledge from language models trained to conceal a secret?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Taboo model organism, a language model fine-tuned to hide a secret word, and demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability techniques (Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) can be used to elicit this hidden knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability-based approaches show promise for eliciting hidden knowledge from LLMs, and the Taboo model provides a useful benchmark for future work on more complex forms of concealed information.
papers.key_findings:
The Taboo model successfully conceals its secret word, resisting direct and adversarial prompting.
Mechanistic interpretability methods (Logit Lens and SAEs) can elicit the secret word from the model's internal representations.
Token forcing is highly effective after the model is 'warmed up' with several turns of gameplay.
A separate LLM (Gemma 3) can guess the secret from the Taboo model's hints, confirming the hints are meaningful.
No evaluated method achieved perfect accuracy, indicating room for improvement in elicitation techniques.
papers.limitation:
The model organism uses a single-token secret word, representing a relatively simple form of hidden knowledge.
No evaluated method achieved near-perfect accuracy, even in this simplified setting.
future_direction: Explore more complex model organisms designed to hide multi-token secrets, abstract concepts, or hidden objectives.
papers.abstract: As language models become more powerful and sophisticated, it is crucial that they remain trustworthy and reliable. There is concerning preliminary evidence that models may attempt to deceive or keep secrets from their operators. To explore the ability of current techniques to elicit such hidden knowledge, we train a Taboo model: a language model that describes a specific secret word without explicitly stating it. Importantly, the secret word is not presented to the model in its training data or prompt. We then investigate methods to uncover this secret. First, we evaluate non-interpretability (black-box) approaches. Subsequently, we develop largely automated strategies based on mechanistic interpretability techniques, including logit lens and sparse autoencoders. Evaluation shows that both approaches are effective in eliciting the secret word in our proof-of-concept setting. Our findings highlight the promise of these approaches for eliciting hidden knowledge and suggest several promising avenues for future work, including testing and refining these methods on more complex model organisms. This work aims to be a step towards addressing the crucial problem of eliciting secret knowledge from language models, thereby contributing to their safe and reliable deployment.

papers.title: Who's the Evil Twin? Differential Auditing for Undesired Behavior
papers.research_question: How can hidden harmful behaviors in neural networks be detected under near-zero knowledge conditions using an adversarial game framework?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces an adversarial game framework for differential auditing of neural networks, showing that gradient-based methods like FGSM and prompt-based strategies like scratchpad hijacking can effectively detect hidden harmful behaviors under near-zero knowledge conditions.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the difficulty of auditing models with near-zero knowledge but identifies effective strategies like adversarial attacks and prompt hijacking, contributing to the design of better audits.
papers.key_findings:
FGSM achieved 100% accuracy in detecting CNN backdoors when using hints, demonstrating the effectiveness of gradient-based attacks.
Scratchpad hijacking successfully revealed hidden instruction sets in blackbox LLMs, indicating vulnerabilities in system message injections.
Architectural differences, such as the presence of LoRA modules, provided clear signals for detecting fine-tuned models in open-weight LLMs.
Standard benchmarks like TruthfulQA yielded only weak signals, highlighting their inadequacy for specific undesirable behavior detection.
Targeted behavioral tests with partial information, such as prompting for cancer stories or brand-related questions, proved effective for uncovering misalignment in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Limited time and computational resources prevented running expensive iterative rounds with full strategy adaptation.
Detection techniques were non-transferable between CNN and LLM architectures, limiting conclusive findings.
Experimental complications, such as unintended architectural asymmetry from single-model LoRA fine-tuning, constrained comparisons.
future_direction: Investigating theoretical foundations underlying gradient-based methods and prompt structures to develop generalizable detection techniques.
Creating automated behavioral testing frameworks for LLMs to detect diverse undesirable capabilities.
Advancing model diffing and attribution techniques that reliably identify and interpret undesirable features in open-weight settings.
papers.abstract: Detecting hidden behaviors in neural networks poses a significant challenge due to minimal prior knowledge and potential adversarial obfuscation. We explore this problem by framing detection as an adversarial game between two teams: the red team trains two similar models, one trained solely on benign data and the other trained on data containing hidden harmful behavior, with the performance of both being nearly indistinguishable on the benign dataset. The blue team, with limited to no information about the harmful behaviour, tries to identify the compromised model. We experiment using CNNs and try various blue team strategies, including Gaussian noise analysis, model diffing, integrated gradients, and adversarial attacks under different levels of hints provided by the red team. Results show high accuracy for adversarial-attack-based methods (100\% correct prediction, using hints), which is very promising, whilst the other techniques yield more varied performance. During our LLM-focused rounds, we find that there are not many parallel methods that we could apply from our study with CNNs. Instead, we find that effective LLM auditing methods require some hints about the undesired distribution, which can then used in standard black-box and open-weight methods to probe the models further and reveal their misalignment. We open-source our auditing games (with the model and data) and hope that our findings contribute to designing better audits.

papers.title: Watch the Weights: Unsupervised monitoring and control of fine-tuned LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we understand and monitor fine-tuned LLMs without access to their training data, especially for detecting backdoors and other anomalous behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces WeightWatch, a method that uses singular vectors of weight differences between fine-tuned and base models to detect and steer anomalous behaviors without access to training data.
papers.conclusion: WeightWatch provides a scalable, data-free approach for interpreting and controlling fine-tuned LLMs, enabling effective detection of backdoors and unlearned content.
papers.key_findings:
WeightWatch detects backdoor utilizations with up to 100% accuracy and false positive rate below 1.2%.
It detects inference on unlearned topics with accuracy up to 95.42%.
